claim: Nannochloropsis oceanica algal cells become internalized within the hyphae of the fungus Mortierella elongata.
source: Here, we report on an algal–fungal interaction in which Nannochloropsis oceanica algal cells become internalized within the hyphae of the fungus Mortierella elongata.
evidence: Supported by microscopy observations including DIC, TEM, and confocal microscopy showing algal cells within fungal hyphae after long-term co-culture.

claim: The symbiosis between N. oceanica and M. elongata begins with close physical contact and nutrient exchange.
source: This apparent symbiosis begins with close physical contact and nutrient exchange, including carbon and nitrogen transfer between fungal and algal cells as demonstrated by isotope tracer experiments.
evidence: Demonstrated through isotope tracer experiments using 14C and 15N showing bidirectional nutrient transfer.

claim: Carbon and nitrogen are transferred between fungal and algal cells during co-cultivation.
source: This apparent symbiosis begins with close physical contact and nutrient exchange, including carbon and nitrogen transfer between fungal and algal cells as demonstrated by isotope tracer experiments.
evidence: Demonstrated by isotope tracer experiments showing 14C-carbon and 15N-nitrogen transfer between partners.

claim: The mutualism between N. oceanica and M. elongata is stable, with both partners remaining physiologically active over months of co-cultivation.
source: This mutualism appears to be stable, as both partners remain physiologically active over months of co-cultivation, leading to the eventual internalization of photosynthetic algal cells, which persist to function, grow and divide within fungal hyphae.
evidence: Supported by long-term co-culture experiments (1-3 months) showing continued viability and growth of both partners.

claim: Photosynthetic algal cells persist to function, grow and divide within fungal hyphae.
source: This mutualism appears to be stable, as both partners remain physiologically active over months of co-cultivation, leading to the eventual internalization of photosynthetic algal cells, which persist to function, grow and divide within fungal hyphae.
evidence: Demonstrated by time-lapse microscopy showing algal cell division within hyphae and chlorophyll autofluorescence indicating functional photosynthesis.

claim: Mutualistic symbioses underlie many evolutionary and ecological innovations including the acquisition of plastids and mitochondria.
source: Mutualisms underlie many evolutionary and ecological innovations including the acquisition of plastids and mitochondria, and evolution of symbiotic mutualisms such as mycorrhizas, lichens and corals (Little et al., 2004; Service, 2011; Tisserant et al., 2013; Spribille et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature on evolutionary biology and symbiosis.

claim: Terrestrialization of Earth has been associated with lineages of early diverging fungi belonging to the Mucoromycota.
source: Terrestrialization of Earth has been associated with lineages of early diverging fungi belonging to the Mucoromycota.
evidence: Based on established scientific understanding of fungal evolution and terrestrialization.

claim: Fungal colonization of land was associated with multiple origins of green algae prior to the origin of embryophytes.
source: However, recent analyses indicate that fungal colonization of land was associated with multiple origins of green algae prior to the origin of embryophytes (Lutzoni et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lutzoni et al., 2018.

claim: Plants were genetically pre-adapted for symbiosis with fungi.
source: Research indicating that plants were genetically pre-adapted for symbiosis with fungi, has renewed interest in fungal-algal associations (Delaux et al., 2015; Spatafora et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Delaux et al., 2015 and Spatafora et al., 2016.

claim: Lichens were estimated to radiate 480 million years ago.
source: The most well-known mutualisms that exist between algae and fungi are lichens, which were estimated to radiate 480 million years ago (Lutzoni et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lutzoni et al., 2018.

claim: Lichen symbiosis allows mycobiont and photobiont symbionts to survive in habitats that would be uninhabitable by either species growing alone.
source: Lichen symbiosis is adaptive in that it allows mycobiont and photobiont symbionts to survive in habitats and environments that would otherwise be uninhabitable by either species growing alone, such as on a rock outcrop or in a desert crust.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of lichen ecology.

claim: Lichenized fungi have multiple independent origins in Ascomycota and Basidiomycota.
source: Lichenized fungi have been shown to have multiple independent origins in Ascomycota and Basidiomycota, and are themselves meta-organisms that include communities of chlorophyte algae, cyanobacteria, in addition to basidiomyceteous yeasts (Spribille et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spribille et al., 2016.

claim: Lichens are meta-organisms that include communities of chlorophyte algae, cyanobacteria, and basidiomyceteous yeasts.
source: Lichenized fungi have been shown to have multiple independent origins in Ascomycota and Basidiomycota, and are themselves meta-organisms that include communities of chlorophyte algae, cyanobacteria, in addition to basidiomyceteous yeasts (Spribille et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spribille et al., 2016.

claim: Reciprocal transfer of carbon and nitrogen was shown for synthetic consortia composed of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and a diverse panel of ascomycete fungi.
source: For example, reciprocal transfer of carbon and nitrogen was shown for synthetic consortia composed of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and a diverse panel of ascomycete fungi, demonstrating a latent capacity of ascomycetous yeasts and filamentous fungi to interact with algae (Hom and Murray, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hom and Murray, 2014.

claim: Ascomycetous yeasts and filamentous fungi have a latent capacity to interact with algae.
source: For example, reciprocal transfer of carbon and nitrogen was shown for synthetic consortia composed of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and a diverse panel of ascomycete fungi, demonstrating a latent capacity of ascomycetous yeasts and filamentous fungi to interact with algae (Hom and Murray, 2014).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of nutrient exchange in synthetic consortia, supported by citation.

claim: The filamentous ascomycetous fungus Alternaria infectoria provisions nitrogen to C. reinhardtii in a long-lived bipartite system.
source: In a separate study, the filamentous ascomycetous fungus Alternaria infectoria was demonstrated to provision nitrogen to C. reinhardtii in a long-lived bipartite system, whereby the nitrogen-starved alga responded favorably to the growing fungus (Simon et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Simon et al., 2017.

claim: A non-lichen algal-fungal mutualism exists involving the chytrid fungus Rhizidium phycophilum and the green alga Bracteacoccus.
source: A non-lichen algal-fungal mutualism was described involving the chytrid fungus Rhizidium phycophilum and the green alga Bracteacoccus providing evidence that early diverging fungi have evolved mutualisms with algae based on solute exchange (Picard et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Picard et al., 2013.

claim: Early diverging fungi have evolved mutualisms with algae based on solute exchange.
source: A non-lichen algal-fungal mutualism was described involving the chytrid fungus Rhizidium phycophilum and the green alga Bracteacoccus providing evidence that early diverging fungi have evolved mutualisms with algae based on solute exchange (Picard et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Picard et al., 2013.

claim: In all known examples of fungal-algal symbioses, algal cells remain external to fungal hyphae and are not known to enter living fungal cells.
source: However, in all known examples of fungal-algal symbioses algal cells remain external to fungal hyphae and are not known to enter living fungal cells.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of fungal-algal symbioses prior to this study.

claim: M. elongata and N. oceanica are biotechnologically important oil-producing organisms.
source: While studying a synthetic co-culture composed of two biotechnologically important oil-producing organisms, the soil fungus Mortierella elongata and the marine alga Nannochloropsis oceanica, we observed an interaction between fungal and algal cells that led to changes in metabolism of both partners (Du et al., 2018a).
evidence: Stated as established fact with citation to Du et al., 2018a.

claim: The biotrophic interaction between M. elongata and N. oceanica shows high specificity.
source: This biotrophic interaction showed high specificity and resulted in close physical contact of partners, with the eventual incorporation of functional algal cells within fungal mycelium.
evidence: Supported by screening experiments showing that only certain Mortierella species interact strongly with N. oceanica.

claim: The biotrophic interaction between M. elongata and N. oceanica results in close physical contact of partners.
source: This biotrophic interaction showed high specificity and resulted in close physical contact of partners, with the eventual incorporation of functional algal cells within fungal mycelium.
evidence: Demonstrated by SEM and other microscopy showing wall-to-wall contact and algal cells attached to hyphae.

claim: The biotrophic interaction between M. elongata and N. oceanica leads to the incorporation of functional algal cells within fungal mycelium.
source: This biotrophic interaction showed high specificity and resulted in close physical contact of partners, with the eventual incorporation of functional algal cells within fungal mycelium.
evidence: Demonstrated by TEM, DIC, and confocal microscopy showing algal cells inside fungal hyphae.

claim: Nannochloropsis oceanica cells flocculated in dense clusters around M. elongata mycelium when co-incubated.
source: Nannochloropsis oceanica cells flocculated in dense clusters around M. elongata mycelium when they were incubated together (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Directly observed and documented in Figure 1A and B.

claim: After 6 days co-cultivation, scanning electron microscopy revealed a wall-to-wall fungal-algal interface between the organisms.
source: After 6 days co-cultivation, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) revealed a wall-to-wall fungal-algal interface between the organisms grown in co-culture, (Figure 1C) with the morphology of N. oceanica cells differing from those of cells grown in the absence of fungus.
evidence: Demonstrated by SEM imaging shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The morphology of N. oceanica cells differs from those of cells grown in the absence of fungus after co-culture with M. elongata.
source: After 6 days co-cultivation, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) revealed a wall-to-wall fungal-algal interface between the organisms grown in co-culture, (Figure 1C) with the morphology of N. oceanica cells differing from those of cells grown in the absence of fungus.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing SEM images of algae grown alone versus in co-culture.

claim: N. oceanica cells incubated alone in f/2 medium have a smooth outer layer.
source: Specifically, SEM images showed that N. oceanica cells incubated alone in f/2 medium have a smooth outer layer (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), which was fragmented or lacking after co-culture with M. elongata AG77 and fibrous extensions underneath the smooth outer layer were exposed (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by SEM imaging shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The smooth outer layer of N. oceanica cells is fragmented or lacking after co-culture with M. elongata AG77.
source: Specifically, SEM images showed that N. oceanica cells incubated alone in f/2 medium have a smooth outer layer (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), which was fragmented or lacking after co-culture with M. elongata AG77 and fibrous extensions underneath the smooth outer layer were exposed (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by SEM imaging shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Fibrous extensions underneath the smooth outer layer of N. oceanica cells are exposed after co-culture with M. elongata AG77.
source: Specifically, SEM images showed that N. oceanica cells incubated alone in f/2 medium have a smooth outer layer (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), which was fragmented or lacking after co-culture with M. elongata AG77 and fibrous extensions underneath the smooth outer layer were exposed (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by SEM imaging shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The fibrous extensions of N. oceanica are present underneath the outer smooth layer.
source: While it is possible that the fibrous extensions have been elicited by the contact with the fungus, remnant pieces of the outer coat covering the underlying extensions are evident in our observations (Figure 1E and F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B). Therefore, it seems likely that these extensions are present underneath the outer smooth layer.
evidence: Inferred from SEM observations showing remnant pieces of outer coat covering the extensions.

claim: The fibrous extensions of N. oceanica appear to contribute to anchoring the algae to hyphae.
source: In addition, the fibrous extensions appeared to contribute to anchoring the algae to hyphae and irregular tube-like extensions were formed between the two interacting cell types (Figure 1F).
evidence: Inferred from SEM observations showing fibrous extensions connecting algae to hyphae.

claim: Irregular tube-like extensions are formed between N. oceanica and M. elongata during interaction.
source: In addition, the fibrous extensions appeared to contribute to anchoring the algae to hyphae and irregular tube-like extensions were formed between the two interacting cell types (Figure 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by SEM imaging shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The fibrous extensions of N. oceanica are only exposed in cells that are in physical contact with live fungal hyphae.
source: Further SEM revealed that the fibrous extensions only were exposed in N. oceanica cells that were in physical contact with live fungal hyphae.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing SEM images of algae in different conditions (with/without physical contact, with live/dead fungi).

claim: N. oceanica cells maintained a smooth outer wall covering when co-cultured without physical contact with live fungi.
source: N. oceanica cells maintained a smooth outer wall covering (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) when they were co-cultured without physical contact with live fungi, and when they were co-cultured with M. elongata mycelium that had been killed in a 65°C water bath.
evidence: Demonstrated by SEM imaging shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: N. oceanica cells maintained a smooth outer wall covering when co-cultured with heat-killed M. elongata mycelium.
source: N. oceanica cells maintained a smooth outer wall covering (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) when they were co-cultured without physical contact with live fungi, and when they were co-cultured with M. elongata mycelium that had been killed in a 65°C water bath.
evidence: Demonstrated by SEM imaging shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A combination of 4% fungal hemicellulase and 2% driselase can partially digest the outer smooth cell wall layer of N. oceanica and expose the fibrous extensions.
source: We demonstrated that a combination of enzymes, including 4% fungal hemicellulase and 2% driselase, could partially digest the outer smooth cell wall layer of N. oceanica and expose the fibrous extensions to mimic the morphological change observed during the physical interaction between live M. elongata and N. oceanica cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by enzyme treatment experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A significant amount of 14C-carbon is transferred from N. oceanica to M. elongata during co-culture.
source: Isotope analyses indicated that a significant amount of 14C-carbon was transferred from the alga to the fungus, and nearly 70% of the total transferred 14C-carbon was incorporated into the fungal lipid pool, with the remaining incorporated into free amino acids (FAAs), proteins, soluble compounds, and carbohydrates (Figure 2A, left).
evidence: Demonstrated by 14C tracer experiments and scintillation counting shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Nearly 70% of the 14C-carbon transferred from N. oceanica to M. elongata is incorporated into the fungal lipid pool.
source: Isotope analyses indicated that a significant amount of 14C-carbon was transferred from the alga to the fungus, and nearly 70% of the total transferred 14C-carbon was incorporated into the fungal lipid pool, with the remaining incorporated into free amino acids (FAAs), proteins, soluble compounds, and carbohydrates (Figure 2A, left).
evidence: Demonstrated by fractionation and analysis of 14C-labeled fungal cells shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 14C-carbon is transferred from M. elongata to N. oceanica during co-culture.
source: Similarly, 14C-carbon transfer was observed from the labeled fungus to its algal recipient (Figure 2A, right).
evidence: Demonstrated by 14C tracer experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Algal cells attached to fungal hyphae acquire more 14C than unattached cells in the supernatant.
source: Fractions of algal cells attached to the fungal hyphae acquired more 14C than unattached cells sampled in the supernatant (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing 14C content in attached versus free algal cells shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Physical contact between N. oceanica and M. elongata is essential for 14C-carbon transfer to the fungus.
source: We observed that the physical contact between the algae and fungus is essential for 14C-carbon transfer to the fungus (Figure 2B and C) but is not necessary for 14C-carbon transfer to the algal cells (Figure 2B and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing 14C transfer in physical contact versus no-contact conditions using membrane inserts, shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Physical contact between N. oceanica and M. elongata is not necessary for 14C-carbon transfer to the algal cells.
source: We observed that the physical contact between the algae and fungus is essential for 14C-carbon transfer to the fungus (Figure 2B and C) but is not necessary for 14C-carbon transfer to the algal cells (Figure 2B and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing 14C transfer in physical contact versus no-contact conditions using membrane inserts, shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: Mortierella is commonly regarded as a saprotroph that acquires carbon from dead organic matter.
source: Considering that Mortierella is commonly regarded as a saprotroph that acquires carbon from dead organic matter (Phillips et al., 2014), we tested whether alga-derived carbon obtained by M. elongata was due to the consumption of algal detritus.
evidence: Supported by citation to Phillips et al., 2014.

claim: M. elongata incorporates only 1.3% of 14C-carbon from dead algal cells, compared to 12.7% from living algal cells.
source: We found that M. elongata incorporates only a small amount (1.3%) of 14C-carbon from dead algal cells, compared to 14C-carbon acquired from living algal cells (12.7%) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing 14C incorporation from heat-killed versus living algal cells shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Algal cells attached to fungal hyphae acquire 2.4% of 14C-carbon from dead fungal cells.
source: In contrast, the algal cells attached to fungal hyphae (Att) and those free in the medium (Free) acquired more 14C-carbon (Att, 2.4%; Free, 15.8%) from dead fungal cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by 14C tracer experiments with heat-killed fungal cells shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Free algal cells in the medium acquire 15.8% of 14C-carbon from dead fungal cells.
source: In contrast, the algal cells attached to fungal hyphae (Att) and those free in the medium (Free) acquired more 14C-carbon (Att, 2.4%; Free, 15.8%) from dead fungal cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by 14C tracer experiments with heat-killed fungal cells shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Over 95% of algal cells remain alive during the period of reciprocal co-cultivation with 14C-carbon-labeled cells.
source: Over 95% of algal cells were alive during the period of reciprocal co-cultivation with 14C-carbon-labeled cells, and no dead fungal cells were observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–I).
evidence: Demonstrated by SYTOX Green staining and confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: No dead fungal cells were observed during the period of reciprocal co-cultivation with 14C-carbon-labeled cells.
source: Over 95% of algal cells were alive during the period of reciprocal co-cultivation with 14C-carbon-labeled cells, and no dead fungal cells were observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–I).
evidence: Demonstrated by SYTOX Green staining and confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Carbon-transfer from N. oceanica to M. elongata is dependent upon physical interaction between living partners.
source: Together these data indicate that carbon-transfer from the alga to the fungus is dependent upon physical interaction between living partners.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing minimal transfer from dead algae and requirement for physical contact.

claim: Algal cells are able to utilize carbon from the fungus regardless of whether the hyphae are alive, dead or physically connected.
source: In contrast, the algal cells are able to utilize carbon from the fungus grown in the same culture regardless of whether the hyphae are alive, dead or physically connected.
evidence: Demonstrated by 14C tracer experiments showing carbon transfer to algae in all conditions.

claim: Nitrogen is a major macronutrient that limits net primary productivity in terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems.
source: Nitrogen is a major macronutrient that limits net primary productivity in terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, especially for microalgae such as N. oceanica (Howarth et al., 1997; Vieler et al., 2012; Zienkiewicz et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature on nitrogen limitation.

claim: 15N-nitrogen is transferred between N. oceanica and M. elongata during co-culture.
source: We detected 15N-nitrogen transfer between algal and fungal partners, irrespective of whether they were in physical contact or not (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by 15N tracer experiments shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: 15N-nitrogen transfer occurs between N. oceanica and M. elongata irrespective of whether they are in physical contact.
source: We detected 15N-nitrogen transfer between algal and fungal partners, irrespective of whether they were in physical contact or not (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by 15N tracer experiments in both physical contact and no-contact conditions shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Over twice as much 15N (~1.6 μmol/mg biomass/d) is transferred from M. elongata to N. oceanica than from N. oceanica to M. elongata (~0.7 μmol/mg biomass/day).
source: Over twice as much 15N (~1.6 μmol/mg biomass/d) was transferred from the 15N-fungus to the algal recipient, than from the 15N-algal cells to the fungus (~0.7 μmol/mg biomass/day; Figure 2E), demonstrating a net nitrogen benefit for the alga when co-cultivated with the fungus.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis of 15N transfer rates shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There is a net nitrogen benefit for N. oceanica when co-cultivated with M. elongata.
source: Over twice as much 15N (~1.6 μmol/mg biomass/d) was transferred from the 15N-fungus to the algal recipient, than from the 15N-algal cells to the fungus (~0.7 μmol/mg biomass/day; Figure 2E), demonstrating a net nitrogen benefit for the alga when co-cultivated with the fungus.
evidence: Inferred from the asymmetric nitrogen transfer rates favoring the alga.

claim: N. oceanica has significantly increased viability when co-cultivated with M. elongata during nitrogen or carbon deprivation.
source: During nitrogen or carbon deprivation in f/2 medium, N. oceanica had significantly increased viability when co-cultivated with M. elongata (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by viability assays using SYTOX Green staining shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: M. elongata releases total organic carbon and dissolved nitrogen into the culture medium when incubated alone in f/2 medium.
source: Element analysis of the culture supernatant showed an increase in total organic carbon and dissolved nitrogen when the living M. elongata hyphae were incubated alone in f/2 medium (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Demonstrated by elemental analysis of culture supernatants shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: The release of nutrients by M. elongata hyphae may explain why physical contact is not required for 14C-carbon transfer from the fungus to the alga.
source: This is indicative of extracellular release of nutrients by the hyphae, and may explain why physical contact is not required for the 14C-carbon transfer from the fungus to the alga.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of extracellular nutrient release and the pattern of carbon transfer.

claim: N. oceanica cells show significantly higher levels of chlorophyll when co-cultured with M. elongata compared to algal cells grown alone after 10-day incubation.
source: In addition, following 10-day-prolonged incubation in regular f/2 medium N. oceanica cells showed significant higher levels of chlorophyll with the presence of M. elongata compared to algal cells grown alone, suggesting that the co-cultured algae likely had a higher photosynthetic capacity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by chlorophyll measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Co-cultured N. oceanica cells likely have a higher photosynthetic capacity than cells grown alone.
source: In addition, following 10-day-prolonged incubation in regular f/2 medium N. oceanica cells showed significant higher levels of chlorophyll with the presence of M. elongata compared to algal cells grown alone, suggesting that the co-cultured algae likely had a higher photosynthetic capacity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Inferred from higher chlorophyll levels in co-cultured algae.

claim: Significant increases in biomass are observed for co-cultured N. oceanica and M. elongata under nitrogen deprivation, but not when grown separately.
source: Significant increases in biomass were observed for the co-cultured alga and fungus, but not when the alga or fungus were grown by themselves (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by biomass measurements using fatty acid biomarkers shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Both N. oceanica and M. elongata benefit from their interaction and nutrient exchanges.
source: Therefore, both partners benefitted in this interaction.
evidence: Inferred from increased biomass and viability of both partners during co-culture under stress conditions.

claim: M. elongata is able to grow in nutrient-deprived conditions (PBS buffer) in the presence of N. oceanica, but not when incubated by itself.
source: M. elongata was able to grow in nutrient-deprived conditions (PBS buffer) in the presence of the algal photobiont, but not when it was incubated by itself in PBS buffer without carbon (Video 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by time-lapse microscopy shown in Video 1.

claim: Mortierella elongata shows the most obvious phenotype of flocculating N. oceanica among the tested fungi.
source: Mortierella elongata showed the most obvious phenotype of flocculating alga, which consisted of algal cells clustered around the fungal mycelium (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by screening 20 phylogenetically diverse fungi shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Aside from a few Mortierella species, interactions between other tested fungi and N. oceanica were neutral or negative.
source: Aside from a few Mortierella species tested, interactions between the other fungi and the alga were neutral or negative.
evidence: Demonstrated by screening experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: N. oceanica cells maintain an intact and smooth outer layer when co-cultured with negatively interacting fungi such as Clavulina sp. PMI390 and Morchella americana GB760.
source: It is worth noting that N. oceanica cells maintained an intact and smooth outer layer when co-cultured with the negatively interacting fungi such as Clavulina sp. PMI390 and Morchella americana GB760 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by SEM imaging shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: After ~1 month of co-culture, algal cells are present inside fungal hyphae.
source: After ~1 month of co-culture, confocal microscopy was used to visualize cells inside the thick aggregates that formed between the alga and the fungus. To delineate cell walls, we used a wheat germ agglutinin conjugate cell wall probe, which binds to N-acetylglucosamine, a component in both the Mortierella and Nannochloropsis cell walls (Javot et al., 2007; Scholz et al., 2014). Microscopic observations indicated the presence of algal cells within fungal hyphae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C and Video 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy with cell wall staining shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C and Video 2.

claim: Wheat germ agglutinin conjugate binds to N-acetylglucosamine, a component in both Mortierella and Nannochloropsis cell walls.
source: To delineate cell walls, we used a wheat germ agglutinin conjugate cell wall probe, which binds to N-acetylglucosamine, a component in both the Mortierella and Nannochloropsis cell walls (Javot et al., 2007; Scholz et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Javot et al., 2007 and Scholz et al., 2014.

claim: Differential interference contrast microscopy shows intact and presumably functional algal cells attached to the hyphal tip after long-term co-culture.
source: Differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy showed the morphology of the 'green hyphae' after long-term co-culture, corroborating the presence of intact and presumably functional algal cells attached to the hyphal tip (Figure 4A) and present inside the fungal hyphal cells (Figure 4B–E and Video 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by DIC microscopy shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Differential interference contrast microscopy shows intact and presumably functional algal cells present inside fungal hyphal cells after long-term co-culture.
source: Differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy showed the morphology of the 'green hyphae' after long-term co-culture, corroborating the presence of intact and presumably functional algal cells attached to the hyphal tip (Figure 4A) and present inside the fungal hyphal cells (Figure 4B–E and Video 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by DIC microscopy shown in Figure 4B–E and Video 3.

claim: The viability of M. elongata is demonstrated by transferring M. elongata-N. oceanica aggregates to fresh PDB/2 plates.
source: The viability of M. elongata was demonstrated by transferring M. elongata-N. oceanica aggregates to fresh PDB/2 plates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by observing new fungal growth after transfer shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy shows algal cells outside of fungal cells surrounded by the fungal mycelium.
source: Algal cells were seen outside of fungal cells surrounded by the fungal mycelium (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I); however, some algal cells are clearly present within the hyphae (Figure 4F and G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by TEM imaging shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy shows some algal cells clearly present within fungal hyphae.
source: Algal cells were seen outside of fungal cells surrounded by the fungal mycelium (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I); however, some algal cells are clearly present within the hyphae (Figure 4F and G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by TEM imaging shown in Figure 4F and G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fungal cytoplasmic contents are visible in fungal cells containing algae, suggesting fungal cells are alive and functional.
source: Fungal cytoplasmic contents were visible suggesting fungal cells containing algae were alive and functional (Figure 4).
evidence: Inferred from TEM observations showing intact fungal cytoplasm in cells containing algae.

claim: Internalization of N. oceanica within M. elongata is preceded by dense aggregation of algal cells around the hyphal tip.
source: We were not able to capture the exact transitional stage of entry of N. oceanica into hyphae of M. elongata by TEM; however, through DIC and time-lapse microscopy, we repeatedly observed that internalization of algae is preceded by dense aggregation of algal cells around the hyphal tip (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by DIC and time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Dense clusters of algal cells at the tip of a hypha are consistently observed when algal cells are found within fungal hyphae growing in semisolid medium.
source: Dense clusters of algal cells at the tip of a hypha were consistently observed when algal cells were found within fungal hyphae growing in a semisolid medium (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by DIC microscopy observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Hyphae proximal from tips with dense algal clusters are often green, and the number of algae within these cells increases over time.
source: Furthermore, hyphae proximal from these tips were often green, and the number of algae within these cells increased over time (Figure 4A–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by DIC microscopy observations shown in Figure 4A–E.

claim: Trapped algal cells are able to grow and divide within their fungal host.
source: In fact, trapped algal cells were able to grow and divide within their host (Video 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by time-lapse microscopy shown in Video 4.

claim: Both fungal host and internalized algae within the hyphae are alive after 1-2 months of co-culture.
source: The results are consistent with the notion that both fungal host and internalized algae within the hyphae are alive (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by SYTOX Green exclusion and chlorophyll autofluorescence shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Algal cells inside green hyphae are surrounded by fungal organelles, especially lipid droplets.
source: DIC microscopy also confirmed that the algal cells inside green hyphae are surrounded by fungal organelles, especially what appear to be lipid droplets (Figure 4—figure supplement 6 and Video 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by DIC microscopy shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6 and Video 5.

claim: The Mortierella-Nannochloropsis interaction differs from lichens in that Mortierella lacks distinct tissue differentiation or hyphal structures.
source: While the apparent fungal-algal symbiosis may conjure the concept of a lichen, it differs in many respects. Mortierella lacks distinct tissue differentiation or hyphal structures (i.e. thallus, haustoria).
evidence: Based on morphological observations and comparison with known lichen structures.

claim: Hyphae of Mortierella harbor algal cells intracellularly while lichens maintain algae in a fungal matrix external to their cells.
source: Moreover, hyphae of Mortierella harbor algal cells intracellularly while lichens maintain algae in a fungal matrix, but external to their cells.
evidence: Based on microscopy observations and established knowledge of lichen structure.

claim: There are no other known examples of fungi that host intracellular eukaryotic photobionts.
source: In fact, we know of no other examples of fungi that have been shown to host intracellular eukaryotic photobionts.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature on fungal-algal symbioses.

claim: Endosymbiosis of living eukaryotic cells by fungal hyphae is not known from nature nor the lab prior to this study.
source: Endosymbiosis of living eukaryotic cells by fungal hypha is not known from nature nor the lab.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature on fungal symbioses.

claim: Geosiphon pyriformis forms a unique intracellular association with the photosynthetic cyanobacterium Nostoc punctiforme.
source: However, Geosiphon pyriformis, an early diverged fungal relative of Mortierella and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, does form a unique intracellular association with the photosynthetic cyanobacterium Nostoc punctiforme (Mollenhauer et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mollenhauer et al., 1996.

claim: In Geosiphon pyriformis, the fungus envelops Nostoc within a specialized swollen multinucleate fungal 'bladder' that is morphologically distinct from the rest of the fungal mycelium.
source: In this fungal-bacterial photobiont symbiosis, the fungus envelops the photosynthetic Nostoc within a specialized swollen multinucleate fungal 'bladder' that is morphologically distinct from the rest of the fungal mycelium (Schüßler et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schüßler et al., 1996.

claim: In Geosiphon pyriformis, cyanobacteria are surrounded by a host-derived symbiosome membrane specialized for acquiring photosynthate.
source: Within this bladder, the cyanobacteria are surrounded by a host-derived symbiosome membrane specialized for acquiring photosynthate (Brenner et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brenner et al., 2008.

claim: The hyphal tip is the actively growing region of the fungal colony and a point of growth, membrane endocytosis, and cell wall construction.
source: The hyphal tip is the actively growing region of the fungal colony, and a point of growth, membrane endocytosis, and cell wall construction (Steinberg, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Steinberg, 2007.

claim: The hyphal tip is hypothesized to be the initial point of entry for algal cells into the hyphae.
source: Ultimately, we hypothesize that the hyphal tip is the initial point of entry for the algal cells into the hyphae, as the hyphal tips are the least differentiated cell features in a mycelial network, and the site of continuous plasma membrane recycling and cell wall generation.
evidence: Inferred from observations of algal aggregation at hyphal tips and knowledge of hyphal tip biology.

claim: Mortierella fungi share habitat and ecological niches with other Chromealveolate and algae.
source: Irrespective of whether the species studied here are ancient fungal-algal symbionts, or whether our findings demonstrate a latent capacity for intricate fungal-algal interactions, Mortierella fungi do share habitat and ecological niches with other Chromealveolate and algae.
evidence: Based on known ecology and distribution of Mortierella and algae.

claim: M. elongata and N. oceanica are globally distributed.
source: Although we have studied these organisms in a synthetic co-culture, given the global distribution of M. elongata and N. oceanica, it is plausible that these organisms (or their relatives) interact naturally, such as in marine tidal zones, estuaries or other ecotones.
evidence: Based on known biogeography of these species.

claim: It is plausible that M. elongata and N. oceanica (or their relatives) interact naturally in marine tidal zones, estuaries or other ecotones.
source: Although we have studied these organisms in a synthetic co-culture, given the global distribution of M. elongata and N. oceanica, it is plausible that these organisms (or their relatives) interact naturally, such as in marine tidal zones, estuaries or other ecotones.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the organisms' distributions and ecological niches.

claim: Many endosymbionts are acquired laterally, such as Symbiodinium photobionts of coral.
source: Many endosymbionts are acquired laterally, such as Symbiodinium photobionts of coral (Mies et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mies et al., 2017.

claim: Some endosymbionts are heritable, such as the bacterial endosymbiont Glomeribacter gigasporarum, which is transmitted in spores of mycorrhizal fungi.
source: Other endosymbionts are heritable, such as the bacterial endosymbiont Glomeribacter gigasporarum, which is transmitted in spores of mycorrhizal fungi (Bianciotto et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bianciotto et al., 2004.

claim: It is possible that internalized algae are transmitted vertically to fungal progeny given the relative sizes of Nannochloropsis cells and Mortierella spores.
source: Given the relative size of Nannochloropsis cells (2–3 μm) to those of sporangiospores (2–3 μm), chlamydospores (23–30 μm) and zygospores (25–38 μm) of M. elongata, it is possible that internalized algae are transmitted vertically to fungal progeny.
evidence: Speculative inference based on size comparisons.

claim: There is no evidence for heritability of internalized algae in Mortierella at this time.
source: However, we have no evidence for heritability at this time.
evidence: Explicit statement of lack of evidence.

claim: Fungi are ubiquitous and function as root symbionts for a majority of land plant lineages.
source: Fungi are ubiquitous and function as root symbionts for a majority of land plant lineages and are regarded as having an essential role in the terrestrialization of Earth (Field et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Field et al., 2016.

claim: Fungi are regarded as having an essential role in the terrestrialization of Earth.
source: Fungi are ubiquitous and function as root symbionts for a majority of land plant lineages and are regarded as having an essential role in the terrestrialization of Earth (Field et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Field et al., 2016.

claim: Mucoromycota is resolved as the earliest monophyletic lineage of plant-associated fungi.
source: Recent phylogenomic analyses of Fungi resolve Mucoromycota as the earliest monophyletic lineage of plant-associated fungi (Spatafora et al., 2016), which include Glomeromycotina (arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi), Mucoromycotina (sugar-fungi), and Mortierellomycotina (soil molds).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spatafora et al., 2016.

claim: Mucoromycota includes Glomeromycotina (arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi), Mucoromycotina (sugar-fungi), and Mortierellomycotina (soil molds).
source: Recent phylogenomic analyses of Fungi resolve Mucoromycota as the earliest monophyletic lineage of plant-associated fungi (Spatafora et al., 2016), which include Glomeromycotina (arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi), Mucoromycotina (sugar-fungi), and Mortierellomycotina (soil molds).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spatafora et al., 2016.

claim: Fungi in the Mucoromycota are characterized by their ability to form intimate cross-kingdom intracellular symbioses.
source: One trait that characterizes fungi in the Mucoromycota is their ability to form intimate cross-kingdom intracellular symbioses, which may be facilitated by the lack of regular septate cross walls between hyphal cells.
evidence: Based on known characteristics of Mucoromycota fungi.

claim: The ability of Mucoromycota to form intimate cross-kingdom intracellular symbioses may be facilitated by the lack of regular septate cross walls between hyphal cells.
source: One trait that characterizes fungi in the Mucoromycota is their ability to form intimate cross-kingdom intracellular symbioses, which may be facilitated by the lack of regular septate cross walls between hyphal cells.
evidence: Speculative inference based on fungal morphology.

claim: Mucoromycota fungi form mycorrhizal symbiosis with extant early diverging plant lineages including hornworts, liverworts and mosses.
source: These fungi form mycorrhizal symbiosis with extant early diverging plant lineages including hornworts, liverworts and mosses (Redecker et al., 2000; Spatafora et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Redecker et al., 2000 and Spatafora et al., 2016.

claim: The radiation of Mucoromycota involved the loss of flagella in this lineage of Fungi.
source: This radiation of Mucoromycota involved the loss of flagella in this lineage of Fungi and was contemporaneous with at least two radiations of green algae prior to the emergence of terrestrial embryophytes (Lutzoni et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lutzoni et al., 2018.

claim: The radiation of Mucoromycota was contemporaneous with at least two radiations of green algae prior to the emergence of terrestrial embryophytes.
source: This radiation of Mucoromycota involved the loss of flagella in this lineage of Fungi and was contemporaneous with at least two radiations of green algae prior to the emergence of terrestrial embryophytes (Lutzoni et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lutzoni et al., 2018.

claim: Mortierella that belong to Mucoromycota interact with the microalgae N. oceanica.
source: We show here that Mortierella that belong to this lineage also interact with the microalgae N. oceanica.
evidence: Demonstrated by the experiments described in this study.

claim: The findings enable future studies on cross-kingdom signaling, and genetic and metabolic factors underlying this symbiosis.
source: This finding enables future studies on cross-kingdom signaling, and genetic and metabolic factors underlying this symbiosis.
evidence: Inference about future research opportunities based on the current findings.

claim: Mortierella ecology has evaded mycologists for centuries.
source: Mortierella ecology has evaded mycologists for centuries.
evidence: Based on historical understanding of Mortierella research.

claim: Mortierella fungi are commonly isolated from soils and plant roots.
source: These fungi are commonly isolated from soils and plant roots (Summerbell, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Summerbell, 2005.

claim: Mortierella has been isolated from strata directly under green macroalgae in Antarctica.
source: They have also been isolated from strata directly under green macroalgae in Antarctica (Furbino et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Furbino et al., 2014.

claim: Mortierella is common within cryptobiotic desert crusts.
source: Mortierella is common within cryptobiotic desert crusts (along with bacteria, algae, and other fungi) (Bates et al., 2010), and M. elongata has even been detected in association with red algae in alpine snow packs (Brown and Jumpponen, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bates et al., 2010.

claim: M. elongata has been detected in association with red algae in alpine snow packs.
source: Mortierella is common within cryptobiotic desert crusts (along with bacteria, algae, and other fungi) (Bates et al., 2010), and M. elongata has even been detected in association with red algae in alpine snow packs (Brown and Jumpponen, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown and Jumpponen, 2014.

claim: Mortierella fungi are commonly regarded as soil saprotrophs in the literature.
source: Although commonly regarded as soil saprotrophs in the literature, our results demonstrate that at least some of these fungi are also involved in biotrophic mutualisms.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature on Mortierella ecology.

claim: At least some Mortierella fungi are involved in biotrophic mutualisms.
source: Although commonly regarded as soil saprotrophs in the literature, our results demonstrate that at least some of these fungi are also involved in biotrophic mutualisms.
evidence: Demonstrated by the experiments in this study showing mutualistic interaction.

claim: An early diverging fungus is adapted to form a biotrophic mutualism with Chromalveolate alga.
source: Although N. oceanica is not a charophyte, the closest algal relative to land plants identified to date, our study shows that an early diverging fungus is adapted to form a biotrophic mutualism with Chromalveolate alga, indicating that algal-fungal mutualisms may be more ancient and diverse than previously recognized.
evidence: Demonstrated by the experiments in this study.

claim: Algal-fungal mutualisms may be more ancient and diverse than previously recognized.
source: Although N. oceanica is not a charophyte, the closest algal relative to land plants identified to date, our study shows that an early diverging fungus is adapted to form a biotrophic mutualism with Chromalveolate alga, indicating that algal-fungal mutualisms may be more ancient and diverse than previously recognized.
evidence: Inferred from the discovery of mutualism between an early diverging fungus and a Chromalveolate alga.

claim: M. elongata is the first taxon in the Kingdom Fungi shown to internalize actively photosynthesizing eukaryotic cells.
source: M. elongata is the first taxon in the Kingdom Fungi that has been shown to internalize actively photosynthesizing eukaryotic cells.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature and the novel findings of this study.
